    Multi-turn chat SFT

    After this lesson you can fine-tune on multi-turn conversations with the loss mask applied to every assistant turn (not just the last), verify the mask, and frame honestly what multi-turn training does and doesn't change about the model's long-conversation behaviour.

    Level: intermediate Read time: ~9 min Prerequisites: SFT with TRL's SFTTrainer Updated: 13 Nov 2026

    Everything in Track 2 so far has trained on single-turn pairs: one user prompt, one assistant reply. Real chat data isn't shaped like that. A support conversation has a system message, several user turns, and several assistant turns — and you want the model to learn how to handle every assistant turn in context, not just the last. Multi-turn SFT is exactly the same training loop with a different loss mask: every assistant turn is supervised, every user / system span is masked.

    The data shape: chat-messages, but longer

    From Lesson 1.20: chat-messages format is a list of {role, content} dicts. The only difference here is more entries.

    raw = [
  {"messages": [
    {"role": "system",    "content": "You are a polite support agent. Be concise."},
    {"role": "user",      "content": "I want a refund."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "I can help — what's the order number?"},
    {"role": "user",      "content": "It's ORD-1234."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Thanks. I see the order. Refund will process in 3-5 days."}
  ]},
  # ... more conversations
]
ds = Dataset.from_list(raw)

    Two messages per conversation become four, six, ten. Sequence lengths grow; you'll usually want a larger max_length than the single-turn lessons used.

    Loss on every assistant turn

    The goal: mask every non-assistant token — system message, user turns, the chat-template role headers, and padding — and supervise each assistant turn's content, including the assistant's earlier replies in the same conversation, not just the final one. That is the usual choice for chat fine-tuning: the model learns how to handle every turn position it'll see in production.

    Lesson 2.10's trick doesn't work here. completion_only_loss only masks prompt-completion rows; on a messages dataset it silently trains on every token, system and user turns included. The setting built for messages data is assistant_only_loss=True. It asks the chat template which tokens belong to the assistant, and the template answers through {% generation %}…{% endgeneration %} tags around each assistant reply. Most stock templates, SmolLM2's included, don't have those tags. TRL patches a few templates it knows; for templates it can't patch, such as SmolLM2's, it raises a ValueError rather than guess. So we write a training copy of SmolLM2's template with the tags added, and check that it renders exactly the same text as the original:

    # SmolLM2's chat template, plus {% generation %} tags around each assistant reply
TRAIN_TEMPLATE = (
    "{% for message in messages %}"
    "{% if loop.first and messages[0]['role'] != 'system' %}"
    "{{ '<|im_start|>system\nYou are a helpful AI assistant named SmolLM, trained by Hugging Face<|im_end|>\n' }}"
    "{% endif %}"
    "{% if message['role'] == 'assistant' %}"
    "{{ '<|im_start|>assistant\n' }}"
    "{% generation %}{{ message['content'] + '<|im_end|>' }}{% endgeneration %}"
    "{{ '\n' }}"
    "{% else %}"
    "{{ '<|im_start|>' + message['role'] + '\n' + message['content'] + '<|im_end|>\n' }}"
    "{% endif %}"
    "{% endfor %}"
    "{% if add_generation_prompt %}{{ '<|im_start|>assistant\n' }}{% endif %}"
)
# the training template must render exactly what the model sees at inference
msgs = raw[0]["messages"]
assert (tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False, chat_template=TRAIN_TEMPLATE)
        == tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False))
tok.chat_template = TRAIN_TEMPLATE

    The end-of-turn token <|im_end|> sits inside the tags on purpose: supervising it is what teaches the model to stop. If you can't change the template, the fallback is the manual mask from Lesson 2.4, extended to every assistant turn: render the conversation up to each assistant reply, and set everything outside the replies to -100.

    The training config is Lesson 2.10's canonical SFT_ARGS with the multi-turn changes on top. Run it in the same session as Lesson 2.10's code (for SFT_ARGS, lora, MODEL_ID and dtype), or paste those blocks first. The base model is reloaded because building Lesson 2.10's trainer injected its LoRA layers into the old one.

    from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID, dtype=dtype)   # a fresh base

args = SFTConfig(**{
    **SFT_ARGS,                               # Lesson 2.10's canonical config, plus:
    "output_dir": "multi-turn-out",
    "per_device_train_batch_size": 4,         # smaller micro-batch: longer sequences ...
    "gradient_accumulation_steps": 4,         # ... same effective batch, 16
    "max_length": 2048,                       # multi-turn conversations need it
    "completion_only_loss": None,             # back to the default; it does nothing on messages rows
    "assistant_only_loss": True,              # supervise only the {% generation %} spans
})

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=args,
    train_dataset=ds,
    processing_class=tok,                     # carries TRAIN_TEMPLATE
    peft_config=lora,                         # the same LoraConfig as Lesson 2.10
)

    Verify the mask — the cheap check that catches the loud bug

    Same check from Lesson 2.4 / 2.10, now more important — run it every time, before you train: pull a batch, decode the unmasked positions, confirm they correspond to assistant turns only.

    # after building the trainer, before .train()
batch = next(iter(trainer.get_train_dataloader()))
ids    = batch["input_ids"][0].tolist()
labels = batch["labels"][0].tolist()

# the tokens the model is supervised on
unmasked = [i for i, l in zip(ids, labels) if l != -100]
print(tok.decode(unmasked))
# Should be every assistant reply, each ending in <|im_end|>:
# "I can help — what's the order number?<|im_end|>Thanks. I see the order. ..."
# If you see user or system text in there, the mask is wrong.

trainer.train()   # only once the mask is right

    Pitfalls specific to multi-turn

    • Context-window pressure. Multi-turn conversations are long. If your max_length is too small, examples get truncated, and because TRL keeps the start of each sequence and cuts the end, the last assistant turn (which often carries the resolution) is what gets cut off. Set max_length from the actual length distribution in your training data, not a guess, and drop or split conversations that still don't fit.
    • Role bleed. If the chat template doesn't have crisp role markers (or your data is missing the explicit role field), the loss mask can leak into user turns and the model starts mimicking the user voice in its replies. The mask-verification check above catches this immediately.
    • Sample composition. Five turns of "OK", "OK", "OK", "OK", "Done." is technically multi-turn data and teaches the model nothing useful. Curate for conversations where each turn carries real signal.

    Honest beat — what multi-turn training doesn't do

    Training on multi-turn data does not make the model "better at long conversations" in some general sense. It makes the model better at your turn structure on conversations resembling the ones in your data. Long-range coherence (remembering what was said 20 turns ago, keeping a stable persona over time) is mostly a property of the base model and its context window — fine-tuning on a few hundred multi-turn examples won't move it. If long-conversation behaviour is your goal, also evaluate broadly on out-of-domain conversations (Lesson 1.22's broad eval); the gains and the regressions both live there.

    Key idea

    Multi-turn SFT is single-turn SFT with a richer mask: every assistant turn is supervised, every user / system span is -100. On chat-messages data SFTTrainer does it with assistant_only_loss=True, but only if the chat template marks the assistant turns with {% generation %} tags; completion_only_loss does nothing there. Beyond that, the changes from single-turn are a larger max_length and a smaller batch. The mask-verification check is still the cheapest catch for the loudest bug.

    Recap

    • Supervise every assistant turn and mask the system message, the user turns and the role headers.
    • assistant_only_loss=True needs {% generation %} tags; for SmolLM2 that means a training copy of its template, checked to render identically.
    • Set max_length from your data: TRL keeps the start of each sequence, so the last turn is the first thing cut.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    Delete the {% generation %} and {% endgeneration %} tags from TRAIN_TEMPLATE, keep assistant_only_loss=True, and build the trainer again. What happens?

    Show answer

    Building the trainer fails with a ValueError saying the chat template is not training-compatible (missing {% generation %} markers) and can't be patched. That's the good outcome: TRL refuses rather than guessing a mask. The quiet failure is the other one, dropping assistant_only_loss as well, which trains on every token. The label dump catches that one.

    Key terms

    Multi-turn SFT
    Fine-tuning on conversations with multiple turns, supervising every assistant turn.
    Per-turn loss mask
    Loss applied to every assistant token in the conversation; user / system / chat-template tokens set to -100.
    Mask verification
    Decoding the unmasked positions of a training batch to confirm they correspond to assistant turns only; cheapest catch for a silent mask bug.
    Role bleed
    Mask leaking into user turns so the model is supervised on (and starts mimicking) user-voice text.
    Context-window pressure
    Long multi-turn conversations approaching max_length; TRL keeps the start and truncates the end, so the final assistant turn is cut first, eating the resolution.
    assistant_only_loss
    SFTConfig field for messages data; supervises only the tokens the chat template wraps in {% generation %} tags, and fails if the template has none.
